The map's label for southern China in 500, eighty years after the Jin dynasty had ended. At that date the south was ruled from Jiankang, modern Nanjing, by the short-lived Southern Qi dynasty, which gave way to the Liang in 502.

These were the Southern dynasties, four Chinese houses that followed the Eastern Jin: the Liu Song from 420 to 479, then the Southern Qi, the Liang and the Chen. Each was founded by a general who seized the throne. Across the Huai River they faced the Northern Wei and its successors.

The south was rich in rice, trade and learning. Emperor Wu of Liang, who ruled for almost fifty years from 502, was a devout Buddhist who filled Jiankang with temples, as Buddhism took deep root in the south. His reign ended in a rebellion that wrecked the capital in 549. In 589 the Sui conquered the Chen, the last southern dynasty, and reunited China.
